newsitem.title: SOUTH AFRICA: S.African black business takes another forward step.
newsitem.headline: S.African black business takes another forward step.

text.p: Black empowerment took another giant leap forward in South Africa on Tuesday when the country's biggest corporation, Anglo American, sold control of a major company to black business in a $630 million deal.
African Mining Consortium, a new black group led by Capital Alliance, bought Anglo's 34.9 percent controlling stake in JCI Ltd.
The deal sees one of the gems of South Africa's pivotal mining industry pass into black hands -- in a major symbol of change in post-apartheid South Africa.

The JCI sale is the second big disposal by Anglo American to black interests after the company recently sold off its 35 percent stake in Johnnies Industrial Corp Ltd (Johnnic) -- an industrial holding concern -- to the National Empowerment Consortium.
"The main thrust in these cases is to make our contribution to black empowerment," Anglo chairman Julian Ogilvie Thompson said on Tuesday when he announced the JCI deal.
The combined JCI and Johnnic deal gives blacks control or influence over companies representing nearly a tenth of the capitalisation of the Johannesburg Stock Exchange.

African Mining Consortium is paying 54.50 rand ($12) a share for the JCI stake, with payment due at the end of February, a 5.50 rand ($1,20) premium to JCI's closing price on the stock exchange on Tuesday.
As in the Johnnic deal, Anglo will retain an interest, holding some 12 percent of JCI.

The deal is also a major coup for Capital Alliance, a relative newcomer to the financial scene, which last month signed up Mark Barnes, formerly deputy managing director and head of treasury at Standard Corporate and Merchant Bank, as its chief executive.
Anglo also said on Tuesday it had no plans to sell off any other assets the size of its Johnnic and JCI stakes.

Ogilvie Thompson said it was unlikely Anglo would take the $458 million from the Johnnic sale or the $630 million from the JCI sale out of South Africa due to the country's current stringent foreign exchange control regulations.
Instead, he said the group was likely to invest its new income in projects within South Africa.
